derivation_notes: The parent already encodes phenomenological speed-dependent dissipation through a saturating factor in the restitution-like transfer term. Here that single-curvature saturation is refined to a finite-capacity law with an added quadratic occupancy in the same nondimensional relative-speed variable, preserving the low-speed limit while steepening the high-speed loss of effective restitution.
change_summary: The assumption changed is the shape of the speed-dependent reduction in effective collision efficiency: a single simple saturation is replaced by a sharper nonlinear saturation in relative speed. This changes the scored mapping itself, making v1_after bend more strongly downward versus |v1_before-v2_before| at higher impact speeds while remaining close to the parent at low speed.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: The collision efficiency reduction with relative speed follows a fixed single-curvature saturation law.
assumption_audit.mechanism: As impact speed rises, contact deformation, micro-slip, and irreversible internal losses can intensify nonlinearly, causing the restitution drop to steepen beyond a single simple saturation profile even when the collision remains instantaneous and one-dimensional.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: In the weak-impact limit Abs(v1_before - v2_before)/(1 + Abs(v1_before - v2_before)) << 1, the added quadratic occupancy is negligible and the successor approaches the parent law to leading order.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed masses and baseline collision_efficiency, the effective loss factor multiplies the closing-speed term through one shared saturating speed dependence, so v1_after changes with a single concavity pattern as |v1_before-v2_before| increases.
response_change.child_relation: Keep the same momentum-transfer structure but replace the single shared speed-saturation shape in the effective restitution with a sharper nonlinear speed dependence, so the drop in effective restitution with increasing |v1_before-v2_before| gains additional curvature while retaining the same low-speed limit.
response_change.observable_effect: Holding m1, m2, collision_efficiency, and reduced_mass_partition_sensitivity fixed, low-speed impacts remain close to the parent, but higher-speed impacts show a stronger-than-parent reduction in rebound/transfer efficiency, producing a more bent v1_after versus relative-speed curve that one parent parameter set cannot match simultaneously at both low and high speeds.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Observable when the relative impact speed spans from small values to order-unity-or-larger values on the parent's current nondimensional saturation scale, with positive finite masses and nonzero closing speed; the contrast is weak in the near-zero-speed limit.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: The same speed-loss mechanism is already active in training through relative-speed variation; the refinement extends it by making the high-speed decline steeper/curvier than the parent's single saturation law while preserving the same low-speed trend.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: Recover the parent by taking the added curvature of the speed-dependent loss law to zero so the effective restitution returns to the parent's original single-saturation dependence on |v1_before-v2_before|.

evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: The refinement changes the functional shape of the speed-dependent transfer law, not just its amplitude. evolution_contract.assumption_after: The collision efficiency reduction with relative speed follows a sharper finite-capacity nonlinear saturation, representing stronger high-speed dissipation than a single-curvature law.

evolution_contract.observable_signature: For fixed m1, m2, collision_efficiency, and reduced_mass_partition_sensitivity, scanning relative speed changes the target mapping itself: both models agree closely near zero closing speed, but the child predicts a steeper, more curved reduction of momentum-transfer efficiency once Abs(v1_before-v2_before) reaches order unity on the parent's saturation scale, so v1_after departs systematically from the parent's single-concavity curve.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set can shift overall restitution level and mass-ratio modulation, but it still imposes one shared speed-saturation shape. evolution_plan.activation_condition: Observable when the relative impact speed spans from small values to order-unity-or-larger values on the parent's current nondimensional saturation scale, with positive finite masses and nonzero closing speed; the contrast is weak in the near-zero-speed limit.
evolution_plan.train_hidden_contrast: The same speed-loss mechanism is already active in training through relative-speed variation; the refinement extends it by making the high-speed decline steeper/curvier than the parent's single saturation law while preserving the same low-speed trend.
evolution_plan.continuation_path: Recover the parent by taking the added curvature of the speed-dependent loss law to zero so the effective restitution returns to the parent's original single-saturation dependence on |v1_before-v2_before|.
evolution_plan.gap_statement: The current model already includes speed-dependent dissipation, but it assumes one universal saturation shape for how impact speed reduces effective collision efficiency across all admissible collisions.
evolution_plan.baseline_assumption: The collision efficiency reduction with relative speed follows a fixed single-curvature saturation law.
evolution_plan.scientific_mechanism: As impact speed rises, contact deformation, micro-slip, and irreversible internal losses can intensify nonlinearly, causing the restitution drop to steepen beyond a single simple saturation profile even when the collision remains instantaneous and one-dimensional.
evolution_plan.rationale: A realistic next refinement is to relax the parent's single-shape speed-loss assumption rather than adding a new process. The parent target mapping already varies with relative speed and mass ratio, but for fixed m1, m2, collision_efficiency, and reduced_mass_partition_sensitivity it imposes one specific concavity in v1_after as |v1_before-v2_before| changes. The child would change the scored mapping itself: as relative speed is varied while masses and parameters are held fixed, v1_after would agree near low speed yet deviate systematically at higher speed through stronger curvature in the effective restitution decline. This is scientifically admissible for rigid-body benchmark collisions interpreted as having phenomenological restitution losses from unresolved deformation and slip. The contrast is observable only when the supplied samples span enough relative-speed range; if all impacts are very weak, the parent and child become hard to distinguish. Because the parent has one shared speed-saturation form, refitting its existing parameters can shift overall level and some mass-ratio weighting but cannot simultaneously match both the low-speed and high-speed portions of a genuinely sharper speed-dependent decline across the same fixed-parameter dataset.

scenario_text: Two rigid bodies undergo a one-dimensional instantaneous collision along their common line of motion. Their masses and incoming velocities are sampled independently, while the baseline collision efficiency is fixed. The target is the post-collision velocity of the first body, determined by momentum transfer and the prescribed loss of relative closing speed.
